Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 1 / 65Qualitative predictors
So far: All variables quantitative in linear regression system
But: Often some predictor variables are qualitative
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 2 / 65Example
Data set Credit was collected in the USA
Contains for a larger number of individuals:
◮Balance (monthly credit card invoice): Response variable, quantit ative
◮Age(age): Predictor, quantitative
◮Cards (number of credit cards): Predictor, quantitative
◮Education (number of years of education): Predictor, quantitative
◮Income (Income in thousands of dollars): Predictor, quantitative
◮Limit (credit card limit): Predictor, quantitative
◮Rating (creditworthiness): Predictor, quantitative

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 6 / 65In addition to quantitative variables: Four qualitative pr edictors:
◮Gender
◮Student
◮Ethnicity
◮Married
Qualitative predictors: Also called factors
Factors assume levels :
◮Gender : Male, female
◮student : Yes, no
◮Ethnicity : Caucasian, African-American, Asian
◮Married : Yes, no
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 7 / 65Qualitative predictor with only two levels
Example balance : Diﬀerence between men and women
Other variables are ignored for the moment
Qualitative predictor with two levels (possible values)
Addition of this variable in regression model very simple
Introducing indicator variable (or dummy variable ) which can only
take two possible numerical values
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 8 / 65Example
ForGender :
xi=/braceleftBigg
1 if i-th person female
0 if i-th person male
Using this variable as an predictor variable in the regressi on model
Model:
yi=β0+β1xi+εi=/braceleftBigg
β0+β1+εiifi-th person female
β0+εi ifi-th person male
β0: Average credit card bills of men
β0+β1: Average credit card bills of women
β1: Average diﬀerence of bills men/women

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 13 / 65Qualitative predictor with more than two levels
Qualitative predictor can have more than two levels
Oneindicator variable for all possible values is not enough
In this situation: Add additional indicator variable

xi2=/braceleftBigg

There is:

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 46 / 65Example: Medical Test
Medical Test: Designed to determine whether a person has a di sease
or not
Naturally this test is not quite accurate:
◮Sometimes indicates disease even though person is healthy
◮It does not indicate disease, even though person is ill
Question:
◮You go to physician and do this test for a deadly disease
◮Test is positive: You have disease according to test but do no t
necessarily have disease
◮What is the probability that you really have disease?
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 47 / 65Notation:
◮D: Person has disease D: Person does not have disease
◮+: Test indicates disease −: Test does not indicate disease
Probabilities in Table are known by experiments:
D D
+ 0.009 0.099
− 0.001 0.891
For example: Probability that person has disease andtest is positive
P(D∩+) = 0 .009
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 48 / 65This probability is quite small
Reason: Only a small proportion of population has disease
Various conditional probabilities:
◮P(+|D): Probability that a ill person is really tested positive
◮P(− |D): Probability that a healthy person is correctly tested neg ative
◮P(D|+): Probability that a person tested positive is really ill
◮etc.
First calculate probability P(+|D):
P(+|D) =P(+∩D)
P(D)=0.009
0.009 + 0 .001= 0.9
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 49 / 65ForP(D) following fact was used:
P(D) =P(D∩+) + P(D∩ −) = 0 .009 + 0 .001
Sum of entries in Table in column D
Patients are tested either positive or negative
Conditional probability P(− |D):
P(− |D) =P(− ∩D)
P(D)=0.891
0.891 + 0 .099= 0.9
Seems that this test is quite accurate
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 50 / 65Ill people are tested positive with 90 % and healthy people ar e tested
negative with 90 %
Reverse question
Suppose you do test and result is positive
What is the probability that you really have disease?
Most people will answer 0 .9 (even physicians)
Do you have to worry a lot and write a will?
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 51 / 65Correct answer is conditional probability P(D|+):
P(D|+) =P(+∩D)
P(+)=0.009
0.009 + 0 .099= 0.08
What does this result mean?
Conditional probability P(D|+) is probability that you are really ill if
test is positive
This probability is only 8 %
If test is positive, you only have disease with probability 8 %
Positive test tells very little about whether you have disea se or not
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 52 / 65Why this surprising result?
Reason: Disease is rare
Numerical example: 100 000 people
◮1000 people have disease (1 %)
◮90 % of these will test positive: 900 people
◮99 000 have not contracted disease
◮10 % of these will test positive: 9900 people
◮Total number of people whose test was positive:
900 + 9900 = 10 800
◮However: Among those who tested positive there are far more h ealthy
people who were falsely tested positive
◮Probability that a person who has tested positive is really i ll:
900
10 800= 0.0833
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 53 / 65Bayes Theorem
Bayes theorem: Describes relation between P(A|B) and P(B|A)
Bayes Theorem
P(A|B) =P(B|A)P(A)
P(B)
Example: Bayes theorem returns same solution as before:
P(D|+) =P(+|D)P(D)
P(+)=0.9·(0.009 + 0 .001)
0.009 + 0 .099=0.009
0.009 + 0 .099= 0.08
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Conditional Probability SA: W09 54 / 65Proof of Bayes Theorem
Apply deﬁnition of conditional probability twice
◮It applies:
P(B|A) =P(B∩A)
P(A)⇒ P(B∩A) =P(B|A)·P(A)
◮And:
P(A|B) =P(A∩B)
P(B)⇒ P(A∩B) =P(A|B)·P(B)
Because A∩B=B∩A, it follows:
P(A∩B) =P(B∩A)
And thus:
P(B|A)P(A) =P(A|B)P(B)
Divide both sides by P(B) and get Bayes theorem:
P(A|B) =P(B|A)·P(A)
P(B)
